common_name: Jyunpaku Okinawan Pure White Bitter Melon

planting.note: Direct-sow (or start indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost in cooler areas) after soil is thoroughly warm, providing a sturdy trellis; in zone 9 this Japanese type thrives in the long, humid summer season.

directions: A Japanese Okinawan heirloom-type bitter melon grown for its smooth, creamy-white, blunt-ended fruit, typically 8-10 inches long, that carries noticeably milder bitterness than the common green Indian and Chinese types. As the fruit fully ripens it develops a sweet, bright-red seed coating that is considered the best-flavored of any bitter melon type when eaten out of hand. Okinawan bitter melon (goya) has long been associated with the traditional Okinawan diet and its reputation for longevity, and the pale, gently bitter fruit is well suited to raw preparations like thin-sliced salads as well as classic stir-fries such as goya champuru. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis and consistently moist, fertile soil for strong summer production in Gulf Coast heat.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jyunpaku Okinawan Pure White Bitter Melon
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Bitter Melon

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil reaches 70°F or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; provide a tall arbor or trellis so the long, pale fruit can hang freely for straight, unblemished pods.

directions: A striking, elongated white bitter melon that dangles from the vine like pale stalactites, reaching about 16 inches long with slender, smoothly ridged, faintly mint-green-tinged white skin. Its bitterness is notably gentler than green-skinned types, making it a good choice for fresh stir-fries and soups where a milder flavor is wanted. Beyond its culinary use, the long, glossy, pale fruit hanging against dense green foliage makes the vine a genuine edible ornamental for an arbor or fence-line trellis, drawing attention in the summer garden even before harvest begins. Give it a tall, sturdy support and steady moisture through the long fruiting season to develop full-length, well-formed fruit.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Long White Reishi Bitter Melon
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Bitter Melon

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil is thoroughly warm, or transplant seedlings started 3-4 weeks earlier; this vigorous hybrid Chinese type climbs quickly and begins bearing large fruit in as little as 50-55 days from transplant.

directions: A widely grown Chinese-type hybrid bitter melon producing large, cylindrical, glossy dark-green fruit with thick, crisp flesh, typically 9-11 inches long and up to 3 inches across, with individual fruits often weighing a pound or more. Its size and thick walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and to the stir-fries and braises common in Cantonese and other Chinese preparations, where the mild-to-moderate bitterness pairs with garlic, black bean sauce, or egg. The vigorous vine grows quickly in hot weather and benefits from a tall, sturdy trellis to support both its rampant growth and the weight of the large fruit. Harvest while the skin is still firm, glossy, and fully dark green, before any yellowing begins, for the best texture and flavor.
sources: Urban Farmer — Tai Guo Gourd Seeds
True Leaf Market — Bitter Gourd Tai Guo Hybrid

planting.note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; Verde Puebla is a traditional Mexican landrace type that continues producing into cool fall weather better than many modern tomatillo selections, and can tolerate a light frost without immediately declining. Plant at least two for cross-pollination.

directions: A traditional Mexican tomatillo landrace from the state of Puebla, producing large, round, golden-green fruit that fills and splits its papery husk with a firmer texture and a sweeter, more lemony tang than many standard green tomatillo selections. The vigorous, sprawling plants bear over a long season and hold up better than most tomatillos to cool weather at the end of the season, continuing to set fruit as temperatures drop and tolerating a light frost without a sharp decline in production. Use the ripe golden-green fruit for a milder, less acidic salsa verde, or harvest slightly underripe for the sharper tartness preferred in some traditional recipes. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two for reliable cross-pollination and stake or cage the sprawling vines to keep fruit off the ground.
sources: Hudson Valley Seed Company — Puebla Verde Tomatillo
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomatillo for Texas

planting.note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes, spacing plants somewhat closer than sprawling types since Rendidora holds an upright habit; plant at least two for cross-pollination.

directions: Rendidora is a Mexican-improved tomatillo selection bred for a notably upright, self-supporting growth habit rather than the sprawling vines typical of most tomatillo varieties, making it easier to manage and harvest in a small garden bed without extensive staking. Its name, roughly translating to high-yielding, reflects its reputation for heavy, dependable fruit set: round, slightly flattened, pale yellow-green fruit that fills its papery husk fully at maturity with the classic tart, citrusy tomatillo flavor. The more compact, upright plants can be spaced closer together than standard sprawling tomatillo types, making Rendidora a good choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast vegetable gardens where space for wide-spreading vines is limited. As with all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals to ensure cross-pollination and fruit set.
sources: Utah State University Extension — Tomatillos in the Garden
